title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like
verifiedBy: LLM review of the romanization, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The neutral word order is the English one — subject, verb, object — so Ya lyublyú chay comes out in the order you already think in. Russian can move the pieces around for emphasis, and M10 shows what that does; nothing in this module needs it.

There is no present-tense "to be". Ya studént is the whole sentence — two words, "I student" — and nothing has been left out. Reaching for a word to fill the gap gives Ya yest' studént, which is the single most English mistake you can make in Russian. Only the PRESENT is empty: the past (byl) and the future (búdu) are real words, and they arrive in M5 and M6.

There are no articles at all. kníga is "book", "a book" and "the book"; nothing on the page tells them apart. That is a whole system with nothing to learn — but the work English gives a and the has to go somewhere, and in Russian it goes into word order: M10 is where that is paid.

A name is given with Menyá zovút — literally "me they-call". It is a fixed phrase, not a sentence you assemble: Menyá zovút Iván is "my name is Ivan", and Moyó ímya — Iván, though grammatical, is not how anyone introduces themselves.

iz ("from") changes the ending of the place after it: Índiya → Índii, Moskvá → Moskvý. Russian has six such endings — cases — and this is the first one you meet. Do not try to work it out here: learn Ya iz … with the shape it takes, and M3 starts teaching the endings properly.

Every noun has a gender, and its ending is the first clue: a consonant at the end means masculine (chay, khleb, yazýk), -a or -ya means feminine (kníga, Moskvá, Índiya), -o or -e means neuter (molokó). The clue is not a law — nouns ending in the soft sign -' can be either and must be learned with their gender, and kófe is masculine in spite of its -e. Learn a noun and its gender together.

The thing you like follows the verb, in the object case: Ya lyublyú chay. In this module the object never actually changes shape, because masculine things that are not alive (chay, yazýk) and neuter things (molokó) look identical in the object case. M3 is where the ending finally moves — and it moves on feminine nouns.

In writing, when both halves of an "X is Y" sentence are nouns, a dash stands where English puts is: Ánna — studéntka. After a pronoun it is left out: Ya studéntka. The dash is punctuation, not a word — it is never said out loud.

words.note: Two words that work as one: zovút is "they call" and menyá is "me" — "they call me …", nobody in particular calling. This, not Moyó ímya, is how a Russian gives a name; learn it whole.
A man's name, carried over unchanged — swap in your own. Russian writes names with a capital letter, exactly as English does.

sentences.trap: Menyá zovút Iván looks like it is missing a verb, so English speakers want to add one: Menyá zovút yest' Iván. There is nothing to add — zovút is already the verb of the sentence.
sentences.sound: me-NYA za-VOOT. The unstressed o of zovút comes out as a short "a" — the acute marks the one vowel in the word that keeps its full value, and everything around it flattens. This is the single most useful pronunciation fact in Russian, and it applies to every word on this rung.

variations.changed: swap the name — Menyá zovút itself never moves
menyá → vas: the same verb, now asking somebody else. M2 takes this apart
menyá → yeyó: the phrase names a third person without changing zovút

mistake.why: Grammatical, and nobody says it — it reads the way "My appellation is Ivan" reads in English. Menyá zovút Iván is the sentence.

sentences.usage: The first line of any introduction, in any register.
sentences.mnemonic: zovút is "they call". Your name is what they call you — menyá zovút.

words.note: "Very", and it sits in front of whatever it strengthens, exactly as in English.
"Pleasant", in the shape Russian uses when there is no particular thing being described — it is the whole reply on its own. M9 builds a family of these: mne khólodno, "to me [it is] cold".

sentences.trap: There is no "it", no "is" and no "to meet you" anywhere in it. English needs four words of scaffolding for a formula Russian says in two.
sentences.sound: O-chen pree-YAT-na. The final -o of priyátno is unstressed, so it comes out as "a"; the ' on the end of óchen' is a soft sign, and it only softens the n in front of it — it is never a sound of its own.

variations.changed: a name after a comma — the standard way to close the formula
drop óchen': shorter and cooler, the same reply with less warmth in it
swap what óchen' strengthens — the frame takes any of these words. M2 teaches khoroshó

mistake.why: The Éhto is English scaffolding creeping in. The formula is two words and stands alone.

sentences.usage: Said on being introduced, immediately after hearing a name. Both people say it.
sentences.mnemonic: Not "nice to meet you" but "very pleasant" — the reaction, with the sentence around it left out.

words.note: One pronoun, three shapes picked by the job: ya acts (Ya studént), menyá is acted on (Menyá zovút), mne is the one something is done to (M9's mne khólodno). English does the same with I / me.
A male student. A woman is studéntka — a different word, not a different ending on this one, and it has its own row on S07. Masculine, because it ends in a consonant.

sentences.trap: English cannot say this sentence: it needs am and it needs a. Russian has neither, and adding either one is wrong — Ya yest' studént and Ya odín studént are both mistakes, not politer versions.
sentences.sound: ya stoo-DYENT. The e after the d softens it, so it is "dyent", not "dent" — a plain e after a consonant always does that, and that softening is what most of this course's e's are doing.

variations.cue: I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: studént → studéntka: the sentence changes with who is speaking, which English never does here
ya → a name: still no verb anywhere in the sentence
ne in front of the missing verb — where nothing is, ne goes before the word it denies. M3 teaches this properly

mistake.why: yest' is a real Russian word, but not this one: the present tense of "to be" simply is not written. Ya studént is the whole sentence.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do — work or study — when you meet someone.
sentences.mnemonic: Two words, two ideas: who, and what. Russian charges you nothing for the "is".

words.note: "From", in the sense of coming out of somewhere. It always changes the ending of the place that follows it — that is not optional and not a style, it is what Russian prepositions do.
India. Índiya is the dictionary shape; Índii is what iz takes (Ya iz Índii) and also what v takes (v Índii, "in India"). Stress stays on the first syllable in both.

sentences.trap: Ya iz Índiya copies the dictionary form straight into the sentence, the way English would. iz never leaves a place unchanged.
sentences.sound: ya eez EEN-dee-ee. iz loses its z sound to an s before some consonants, but before a vowel — as here — it stays a clean z.

variations.changed: swap the place — Rossíya shifts to Rossíi exactly as Índiya shifted
ya → a name: the place keeps its iz-shape whoever is speaking
a question with nothing moved — only the mark and the voice change. M2's lesson

mistake.why: iz takes a changed ending, always: Ya iz Índii. The dictionary form Índiya is for the subject of a sentence, not for after a preposition.

sentences.usage: Where you are from — the second or third line of any introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: iz pulls something OUT of a place, and pulling it out bends the ending.

words.note: Moscow. Moskvá is the dictionary and subject shape; Moskvý is what iz takes, and Moskvé what v takes for "in Moscow" (M7). All three keep the stress on the final vowel.

sentences.trap: The two iz sentences take different endings — Índii but Moskvý — and there is no way to guess which from English. The ending depends on how the word itself ends, and this level teaches the pairs rather than the system.
sentences.sound: ya eez mask-VY. The acute says the stress is on the last syllable and the first o is unstressed, so nobody says "MOSS-cow". The ý is the letter Russian writes ы — a hard, back "i" made with the tongue pulled away from the teeth — and it turns up again, stressed, in yazýk.

variations.changed: ya → a name, and still no verb in the sentence
back to the dictionary shape — with no preposition in front of it, Moskvá does not bend
the same words as a question: nothing moves, only the mark

mistake.why: iz bends the place after it. Ya iz Moskvý — and the -ý here is a different ending from Índii's -i, because the two words end differently.

sentences.usage: Naming a city rather than a country — the same frame, and it is the more common answer.
sentences.mnemonic: Moskvá has an a on the end; iz swaps that a for ý.

words.note: The pointing word, and it does the whole job alone: Éhto Ánna is "this is Anna" with no verb. It never changes shape when it opens a sentence — Éhto kníga, Éhto molokó.
A woman's name. Both n letters are written and both are said — a held "nn", not the single n of English "Anna".

sentences.trap: English needs is here and cannot drop it. Russian supplies Éhto and stops — putting anything between Éhto and the name is the mistake.
sentences.sound: E-ta AN-na. The final o of Éhto is unstressed, so it is "E-ta"; the eh is this course's spelling for a letter that is always a plain, open "e" and never softens the consonant in front of it. The double n of Ánna is genuinely held, roughly "AN-na".

variations.changed: swap who is being introduced — Éhto never moves
point at a role instead of a person — and there is still no word for "a"
the same two words asked instead of told — Russian moves nothing to make a question

mistake.why: The same reflex as Ya yest' studént, one sentence later. Éhto Ánna is complete.

sentences.usage: Introducing somebody else, or pointing at a thing and naming it.
sentences.mnemonic: Éhto points, and pointing is enough — Russian does not also need to say that the thing is.

words.note: A female student — its own word, studént with -ka, feminine because it ends in -a. Russian names most jobs twice like this; pick by who is described, not who speaks.

sentences.trap: The dash is not a translation of is. It is a punctuation mark that marks the gap where English would put a verb, and it appears only when both halves are nouns — never after ya or vy.
sentences.sound: AN-na stoo-DYENT-ka. Nothing is said where the dash is: it is a pause at most.

variations.changed: the same frame about a man — studéntka → studént

variations.cue: I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: a pronoun subject, so the dash goes: it is written only between two nouns

variations.cue: Anna is a student from Moscow
variations.changed: the iz phrase hangs off the second noun, exactly as in English

mistake.why: The dash belongs between two nouns. With a pronoun in front, Russian writes Ya studéntka and nothing else.

sentences.usage: Saying what somebody else does — the third line of an introduction, after their name.
sentences.mnemonic: Two nouns need something between them, so Russian draws a line where English says is.

words.note: One verb for "like" and "love"; about food it is simply "like". The ending names who: lyublyú (I), lyúbit (he or she), lyúbite (you) — and the stress moves with it. The b is an I-form quirk.
Tea. Masculine, because it ends in a consonant sound — and because it is a thing rather than a living creature, it looks exactly the same as the object of a sentence as it does in the dictionary.

sentences.trap: lyublyú is not too strong. English keeps love for people and big feelings, so "I love tea" sounds odd; Russian uses lyublyú for anything you are fond of, and saying it about tea is completely ordinary.
sentences.sound: ya lyoo-BLYOO chai. The l is soft in both syllables — the tongue is up against the roof of the mouth, closer to English "million" than to "loop".

variations.changed: lyublyú → lyúbit: the ending swaps the person, the stress moves back with it, and no other word moves
lyublyú → lyúbite for the person you are speaking to, and the sentence becomes a question with nothing added
a describing word slots in front of the noun, exactly where English puts it

mistake.why: chay does not change here. Bending the ending is what M3's feminine nouns do; a masculine thing like chay stays as it is.

sentences.usage: Likes of every kind — food, drink, music, a language.
sentences.mnemonic: lyublyú covers everything from tea to people; Russian simply does not have a weaker word for it.

words.note: Milk. Neuter, because it ends in -o — and neuter things look identical as subject or object, so molokó does not move here.

sentences.trap: There is no "the" and no "some" in front of it. Ya lyublyú molokó covers "I like milk" in general, which is the only reading this sentence has.
sentences.sound: ma-la-KO. Three o's, and only the one under the acute is really an "o" — the other two flatten to "a". The acute is doing you a favour a Russian book will not: real print leaves the stress unmarked and expects you to know it already.

variations.changed: lyublyú → lyúbit: the person changes and molokó does not
the polite you-form, asked rather than told
the same word as the subject of a pointing sentence — proof that it never bends

mistake.why: A neuter noun does not change in the object slot. Ya lyublyú molokó — moloká is a different shape with a different job, and this sentence has no use for it.

sentences.usage: Everyday likes and dislikes about food and drink.
sentences.mnemonic: Neuter nouns are the lazy ones: subject or object, they never get up.

words.note: "Russian" as a description, in front of what it describes, as in English. Russian writes nationalities and languages with a small letter — rússkiy, never Rússkiy.
Language — and also the tongue in your mouth, the same double meaning English once had. Masculine, ends in a consonant, and does not change in the object slot.

sentences.trap: The language is rússkiy yazýk, two words, and dropping the noun does not work the way "I like Russian" does in English. Rússkiy on its own describes a Russian man.
sentences.sound: ROO-skee ya-ZYK. The double s of rússkiy is one long "ss", and the ý of yazýk is that hard back "i" from Moskvý again, stressed this time.

variations.changed: lyublyú → lyúbit, and the two-word object travels together

variations.cue: Do you like the Russian language?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, as a question
swap the noun and rússkiy comes along unchanged, because chay is masculine too

mistake.why: Two things at once: languages take a small letter in Russian, and the noun yazýk cannot be dropped. Ya lyublyú rússkiy yazýk.

sentences.usage: Saying what you study or what you are here for — the natural last line of a first introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: rússkiy is the coat and yazýk is the person wearing it; Russian never sends the coat out alone.

comprehensionPool.cue: I am a student (a woman speaking)
